candidates.comment:
The PFC circuit is pointless. A sinusoidal voltage and a sinusoidal current create a (1-(cos (2*Pi*f*t))²) power function which is of course not constant. How to achieve constant power (ie voltage) at the output, if the input power has a pulsating form?
This means that the PFC circuit cannot be a DC voltage pre-regulator as is often used. When it is a pre-regulator, it would have to draw constant power at constant consumption. And this would tend to create a current function of the form: I(t)=P/(A*sin(2*Pi*f*t)) which would draw a large current at low voltage points to maintain constant power. Such a current function increases the effective current through the conductors and creates additional transmission losses.
The best point of consumption for the smallest current through the conductors is at the top of the sinusoidal function. And the best PFC corrector is an LC filter after the diode rectifier, which suppresses the high harmonics of impulse current disturbances, i.e. reduces the current peak and extends the duration.

PFC only makes sense on machines that have sinusoidal current consumption that is out of phase with the voltage. And these circuits are called reactive power compensators.

There is also no conclusion from the measurement that the installation of the PFC circuit increased the effective input current by more than 10%. Because of this, losses in electricity transmission increase by more than 20%.

candidates.comment:
Interesting factoid about PFC: in the past, unscrupulous people used to tamper with their inductive loads, such as washing machines, pumps, and other motors and REMOVE the PFC capacitor in order to steal part of the electricity from the power company!
This is because power companies used to measure their customers' energy consumption using electromechanical meters, old devices containing a big spinning wheel that would complete a revolution after a known amount of energy was delivered to the customer, plus an odometer to count the wheel's revolutions.
One problem with those electromechanical meters (that has since been solved with digital energy meters) is that they would only measure the current delivered IN PHASE with the voltage. Large inductive loads, such as motors, were (and still are) required by law to be sold with a suitable capacitor as a passive PFC. But if one removed the capacitor, a good part of that load would become undetectable by the energy meter!
This is of course illegal and detrimental to the power grid, so nobody should attempt to do it, except in a laboratory condition.

candidates.comment:
Active PFC circuits can be very difficult in terms of managing conducted EMI/RFI. You are basically chopping the rectified AC input at a frequency that could be anywhere from a few tens of kHz to a few hundred kHz. In the interest of efficiency the rise and fall times are very short, so there is lots of high frequency content. Some PFC controllers operate at fixed frequency, others at variable frequency. I used to do designs using a controller that I ran at 100 kHz, which at the time was a reasonable compromise when FETs, rectifiers, inductor cores and inductor windings were considered (I often say that in switchers everything is in conflict with everything else).
Filtering ahead of the rectifier will certainly require a reasonbly "large" common mode inductor and some normal mode inductance might be necessary, too. I've seen designs using two common mode inductors.

Radiated EMI/RFI is always a concern in any switecher. Circuit layout needs to be carefully considered.

I noted that at some point in the video there was a huge amount of "fur" on the waveform shown on the oscilloscope.

The mention of inductive and capacitive elements, as well as zero net reactance, shows strong overlap with the topic.
candidates.comment:
It's shuffled between energy storage elements within the AC waveform cycle.   Inductive elements store energy in their core magnetic field, and capacitive elements store energy in the dielectric's electric field.  These elements cause current to either lead voltage or lag voltage.   The other type of element can correct power factor, since an inductor and capacitor combined at the right frequency, have zero net reactance, as the rest of the circuit experiences.

This causes the apparent product of current and voltage, to be more than the actual power that enters the electrical domain at the source, and exits the electrical domain to the load.

candidates.comment:
@eDoc2020  "Negative power factor" is a misleading term.  Even though cos(phi) is always positive for loads, and negative for sources, there is a sign convention that artificially adds another sign on top of the sign of cos(phi).

Quadrant 1 is inductive loads with positive reactive power (VARs), and quadrant 4 is capacitive loads with negative reactive power (VARs).   It's quadrants 2 and 3 that are sources, rather than loads.  Quadrant 2 supports capacitive loads, and quadrant 3 supports inductive loads.

IEEE assigns quadrants 1 and 3 as negative power factor, and quadrants 2 and 4 as positive power factor.
IEC assigns quadrants 1 and 3 as positive power factor, and quadrants 2 and 4 as negative power factor.

candidates.comment: Yes, PFC's perform well.  However, they have the same inrush problem on power application as putting a large cap directly across the input line.  In your demo board schematic the C2 cap is, effectively, across the input line if you trace back through the D1, D2, and bridge rectifier.  There is no real current limit when line voltage is applied.  Not even RT1 is wholly effective.  After the boost has time to charge C2 then everything works O.K.  This initial current will depend on where in the mains cycle the circuit is switched on.  I am finding that most of the LED lights with or without PFC have a large input cap that must be charged.  This external cap is effectively in parallel with C2.  The result can be a very large resulting cap that must be charged when power is switched.  An installation of several or many LED arrays can mean very high peak current.  I have measured hundreds of amps peak when an array is switched on.  Not every time, but always on the peak of the sine wave input.  This leads to very short switch life.  It also has the effect of "spot welding" and therefore oxidizing wiring splices or connections that do not have enough contact area.   I have stopped using the "clamp style" (Wago style?) splice devices because of this and gone back to twisting all connections and using a wire nut.  I wish the clamp type connectors were tested and rated for these conditions.  As for the switches?  Expect frequent failures.

The PFC circuit is pointless. A sinusoidal voltage and a sinusoidal current create a (1-(cos (2*Pi*f*t))²) power function which is of course not constant. How to achieve constant power (ie voltage) at the output, if the input power has a pulsating form?
This means that the PFC circuit cannot be a DC voltage pre-regulator as is often used. When it is a pre-regulator, it would have to draw constant power at constant consumption. And this would tend to create a current function of the form: I(t)=P/(A*sin(2*Pi*f*t)) which would draw a large current at low voltage points to maintain constant power. Such a current function increases the effective current through the conductors and creates additional transmission losses.
The best point of consumption for the smallest current through the conductors is at the top of the sinusoidal function. And the best PFC corrector is an LC filter after the diode rectifier, which suppresses the high harmonics of impulse current disturbances, i.e. reduces the current peak and extends the duration.

PFC only makes sense on machines that have sinusoidal current consumption that is out of phase with the voltage. And these circuits are called reactive power compensators.

There is also no conclusion from the measurement that the installation of the PFC circuit increased the effective input current by more than 10%. Because of this, losses in electricity transmission increase by more than 20%.

This is because power companies used to measure their customers' energy consumption using electromechanical meters, old devices containing a big spinning wheel that would complete a revolution after a known amount of energy was delivered to the customer, plus an odometer to count the wheel's revolutions.
One problem with those electromechanical meters (that has since been solved with digital energy meters) is that they would only measure the current delivered IN PHASE with the voltage. Large inductive loads, such as motors, were (and still are) required by law to be sold with a suitable capacitor as a passive PFC. candidates.comment:
Active PFC circuits can be very difficult in terms of managing conducted EMI/RFI. You are basically chopping the rectified AC input at a frequency that could be anywhere from a few tens of kHz to a few hundred kHz. In the interest of efficiency the rise and fall times are very short, so there is lots of high frequency content. Some PFC controllers operate at fixed frequency, others at variable frequency. I used to do designs using a controller that I ran at 100 kHz, which at the time was a reasonable compromise when FETs, rectifiers, inductor cores and inductor windings were considered (I often say that in switchers everything is in conflict with everything else).
Filtering ahead of the rectifier will certainly require a reasonbly "large" common mode inductor and some normal mode inductance might be necessary, too. I've seen designs using two common mode inductors.

Radiated EMI/RFI is always a concern in any switecher. Circuit layout needs to be carefully considered.

I noted that at some point in the video there was a huge amount of "fur" on the waveform shown on the oscilloscope.

candidates.comment:
Power factor is something most people don't worry about because power companies don't bother residential customers about it.  Business customers are scrutinized, and they are penalized if they can't keep the PF above 0.75, or in some places, 0.90, but that's usually only a concern for the building manager.  Historically, business customers had equipment with electric motors (basically inductors) that lowered the PF, while residential customers had mostly resistive lighting and heating with a few motors that turned on periodically (refrigerator, AC, washing machines, etc.).  However, resistive lighting and heating has almost disappeared, replaced by LEDs and heat pumps, and now almost everything we use has an electronic power supply, full of capacitors and inductors.  I don't know what my home's PF is, and the electronic electricity meter that replaced the old analog one doesn't say, but I wouldn't be surprised if that changed.  After all, if power companies switch to time-of-use pricing to reduce maximum demand, they're going to be interested in raising a customers PF for the same reason.
   What really bugs me are LED light bulbs.  The whole point of LED light bulbs is to reduce electricity usage, but manufacturers aren't letting that happen.  Only one watt is needed to produce 200 lumens, but most of the light bulbs I've tested (in the US) get 100 lumens/watt at best.  The excess is turned into heat.  I've measured surface temperatures of over 200 deg F/90 deg C on many bulbs, and the only reason for making them get that hot is to keep the bulb from lasting for a long time.  Heat is the enemy of electronics, but LEDs are cold devices, and especially sensitive to too much heat.  On top of that, most LED light bulbs have a PF of around 0.5, which means the power company has to generate 2 watts for every watt used by the bulb; the extra watt is turned into heat in the power lines.  In extreme cases, this extra heat causes power lines to sag an unsafe amount.  To sum it up, most LED light bulbs, which we use to minimize power usage and reduce global warming, USE 4 TIMES THE ELECTRICITY THAT THEY NEED.  And while most bulbs are less than 20 watts, and used for only a few hours a day in homes, there are millions of them on at any given time.  It adds up.   (I understand the EU has implemented or is implementing requirements that LED light bulbs get 200 lumens/watt.)

candidates.comment: Yes, PFC's perform well.  However, they have the same inrush problem on power application as putting a large cap directly across the input line.  In your demo board schematic the C2 cap is, effectively, across the input line if you trace back through the D1, D2, and bridge rectifier.  There is no real current limit when line voltage is applied.  Not even RT1 is wholly effective.  After the boost has time to charge C2 then everything works O.K.  This initial current will depend on where in the mains cycle the circuit is switched on.  I am finding that most of the LED lights with or without PFC have a large input cap that must be charged.  This external cap is effectively in parallel with C2.  The result can be a very large resulting cap that must be charged when power is switched.  An installation of several or many LED arrays can mean very high peak current.  I have measured hundreds of amps peak when an array is switched on.  Not every time, but always on the peak of the sine wave input.  This leads to very short switch life.  It also has the effect of "spot welding" and therefore oxidizing wiring splices or connections that do not have enough contact area.   I have stopped using the "clamp style" (Wago style?) splice devices because of this and gone back to twisting all connections and using a wire nut.  I wish the clamp type connectors were tested and rated for these conditions.  As for the switches?  Expect frequent failures.

candidates.comment:
It's shuffled between energy storage elements within the AC waveform cycle.   Inductive elements store energy in their core magnetic field, and capacitive elements store energy in the dielectric's electric field.  These elements cause current to either lead voltage or lag voltage.   The other type of element can correct power factor, since an inductor and capacitor combined at the right frequency, have zero net reactance, as the rest of the circuit experiences.

This causes the apparent product of current and voltage, to be more than the actual power that enters the electrical domain at the source, and exits the electrical domain to the load.

That was back when I first undertook the design of a 1kW switcher for a highly specialized purpose and used the Untrode UC3854 for PFC. The 3854 performed really well but the development was pretty painful. There were no development boards around. Just procuring things like inductor cores (I used "Kool Mu", which was pretty new at the time) and high-performance capacitors was a whole lot more complicated and time consuming than it is now. (If I were doing the design now I'd probably go with a PFC stage that used two interleaved converters. They have some significant advantages in situations were high performance and very long service life are necessary.)

One "trick" of active PFC is that the instantaneous input current must be made to be directly proportional to the instantaneous input voltage while the average input current must be made inversely proportional to the input voltage.

candidates.reason: The comment discusses specific aspects of active PFC IC usage, such as managing conducted EMI/RFI, frequency selection (e.g., 100 kHz), and common mode inductance requirements, which directly relates to the topic's description of using an active PFC IC with external components.
candidates.comment:
Active PFC circuits can be very difficult in terms of managing conducted EMI/RFI. You are basically chopping the rectified AC input at a frequency that could be anywhere from a few tens of kHz to a few hundred kHz. In the interest of efficiency the rise and fall times are very short, so there is lots of high frequency content. Some PFC controllers operate at fixed frequency, others at variable frequency. I used to do designs using a controller that I ran at 100 kHz, which at the time was a reasonable compromise when FETs, rectifiers, inductor cores and inductor windings were considered (I often say that in switchers everything is in conflict with everything else).
Filtering ahead of the rectifier will certainly require a reasonbly "large" common mode inductor and some normal mode inductance might be necessary, too. I've seen designs using two common mode inductors.

Radiated EMI/RFI is always a concern in any switecher. Circuit layout needs to be carefully considered.

I noted that at some point in the video there was a huge amount of "fur" on the waveform shown on the oscilloscope.

candidates.comment:
Interesting factoid about PFC: in the past, unscrupulous people used to tamper with their inductive loads, such as washing machines, pumps, and other motors and REMOVE the PFC capacitor in order to steal part of the electricity from the power company!
This is because power companies used to measure their customers' energy consumption using electromechanical meters, old devices containing a big spinning wheel that would complete a revolution after a known amount of energy was delivered to the customer, plus an odometer to count the wheel's revolutions.
One problem with those electromechanical meters (that has since been solved with digital energy meters) is that they would only measure the current delivered IN PHASE with the voltage. Large inductive loads, such as motors, were (and still are) required by law to be sold with a suitable capacitor as a passive PFC. But if one removed the capacitor, a good part of that load would become undetectable by the energy meter!
This is of course illegal and detrimental to the power grid, so nobody should attempt to do it, except in a laboratory condition.

candidates.comment: Yes, PFC's perform well.  However, they have the same inrush problem on power application as putting a large cap directly across the input line.  In your demo board schematic the C2 cap is, effectively, across the input line if you trace back through the D1, D2, and bridge rectifier.  There is no real current limit when line voltage is applied.  Not even RT1 is wholly effective.  After the boost has time to charge C2 then everything works O.K.  This initial current will depend on where in the mains cycle the circuit is switched on.  I am finding that most of the LED lights with or without PFC have a large input cap that must be charged.  This external cap is effectively in parallel with C2.  The result can be a very large resulting cap that must be charged when power is switched.  An installation of several or many LED arrays can mean very high peak current.  I have measured hundreds of amps peak when an array is switched on.  Not every time, but always on the peak of the sine wave input.  This leads to very short switch life.  It also has the effect of "spot welding" and therefore oxidizing wiring splices or connections that do not have enough contact area.   I have stopped using the "clamp style" (Wago style?) splice devices because of this and gone back to twisting all connections and using a wire nut.  I wish the clamp type connectors were tested and rated for these conditions.  As for the switches?  Expect frequent failures.

candidates.reason: The comment directly discusses the use of PFC ICs to achieve constant power and addresses specific design considerations, such as sinusoidal voltage and current, harmonic suppression, and reactive power compensation.
candidates.comment:
The PFC circuit is pointless. A sinusoidal voltage and a sinusoidal current create a (1-(cos (2*Pi*f*t))²) power function which is of course not constant. How to achieve constant power (ie voltage) at the output, if the input power has a pulsating form?
This means that the PFC circuit cannot be a DC voltage pre-regulator as is often used. When it is a pre-regulator, it would have to draw constant power at constant consumption. And this would tend to create a current function of the form: I(t)=P/(A*sin(2*Pi*f*t)) which would draw a large current at low voltage points to maintain constant power. Such a current function increases the effective current through the conductors and creates additional transmission losses.
The best point of consumption for the smallest current through the conductors is at the top of the sinusoidal function. And the best PFC corrector is an LC filter after the diode rectifier, which suppresses the high harmonics of impulse current disturbances, i.e. reduces the current peak and extends the duration.

PFC only makes sense on machines that have sinusoidal current consumption that is out of phase with the voltage. And these circuits are called reactive power compensators.

There is also no conclusion from the measurement that the installation of the PFC circuit increased the effective input current by more than 10%. Because of this, losses in electricity transmission increase by more than 20%.

candidates.comment:
It's an inefficiency in the utility's business model to only bill you for active power.  Poor power factor contributes to increased operating expenses of the grid, that are not reflected in the real power your utility measures.  Displacement power is easy to correct for, since you can simply add the opposite circuit element from the problem type of power factor.  Distortion power is much more difficult to correct for, at the utility scale.

It's common that larger customers are billed for power factor and/or reactive power, while for residential customers, it is difficult to justify the expense of upgrading the meter.  That said, it's only a matter of time until there is enough saturation of non-linear loads for it to become a problem that they eventually have to start reflecting in billing, as a motive to the consumer solve the problem.

candidates.comment:
@eDoc2020  "Negative power factor" is a misleading term.  Even though cos(phi) is always positive for loads, and negative for sources, there is a sign convention that artificially adds another sign on top of the sign of cos(phi).

Quadrant 1 is inductive loads with positive reactive power (VARs), and quadrant 4 is capacitive loads with negative reactive power (VARs).   It's quadrants 2 and 3 that are sources, rather than loads.  Quadrant 2 supports capacitive loads, and quadrant 3 supports inductive loads.

IEEE assigns quadrants 1 and 3 as negative power factor, and quadrants 2 and 4 as positive power factor.
IEC assigns quadrants 1 and 3 as positive power factor, and quadrants 2 and 4 as negative power factor.

candidates.reason: The comment discusses power factor correction and its relation to power consumption, specifically mentioning PF values and how it affects energy efficiency.
candidates.comment:
Power factor is something most people don't worry about because power companies don't bother residential customers about it.  Business customers are scrutinized, and they are penalized if they can't keep the PF above 0.75, or in some places, 0.90, but that's usually only a concern for the building manager.  Historically, business customers had equipment with electric motors (basically inductors) that lowered the PF, while residential customers had mostly resistive lighting and heating with a few motors that turned on periodically (refrigerator, AC, washing machines, etc.).  However, resistive lighting and heating has almost disappeared, replaced by LEDs and heat pumps, and now almost everything we use has an electronic power supply, full of capacitors and inductors.  I don't know what my home's PF is, and the electronic electricity meter that replaced the old analog one doesn't say, but I wouldn't be surprised if that changed.  After all, if power companies switch to time-of-use pricing to reduce maximum demand, they're going to be interested in raising a customers PF for the same reason.
   What really bugs me are LED light bulbs.  The whole point of LED light bulbs is to reduce electricity usage, but manufacturers aren't letting that happen.  Only one watt is needed to produce 200 lumens, but most of the light bulbs I've tested (in the US) get 100 lumens/watt at best.  The excess is turned into heat.  I've measured surface temperatures of over 200 deg F/90 deg C on many bulbs, and the only reason for making them get that hot is to keep the bulb from lasting for a long time.  Heat is the enemy of electronics, but LEDs are cold devices, and especially sensitive to too much heat.  On top of that, most LED light bulbs have a PF of around 0.5, which means the power company has to generate 2 watts for every watt used by the bulb; the extra watt is turned into heat in the power lines.  In extreme cases, this extra heat causes power lines to sag an unsafe amount.  To sum it up, most LED light bulbs, which we use to minimize power usage and reduce global warming, USE 4 TIMES THE ELECTRICITY THAT THEY NEED.  And while most bulbs are less than 20 watts, and used for only a few hours a day in homes, there are millions of them on at any given time.  It adds up.   (I understand the EU has implemented or is implementing requirements that LED light bulbs get 200 lumens/watt.)

candidates.reason: The comment directly discusses the same topic of power factor correction (PFC), its limitations, and the importance of sinusoidal current consumption in relation to PFC circuits. It also specifically mentions the conclusion that PFC only makes sense on machines with sinusoidal current consumption out of phase with voltage.
candidates.comment:
The PFC circuit is pointless. A sinusoidal voltage and a sinusoidal current create a (1-(cos (2*Pi*f*t))²) power function which is of course not constant. How to achieve constant power (ie voltage) at the output, if the input power has a pulsating form?
This means that the PFC circuit cannot be a DC voltage pre-regulator as is often used. When it is a pre-regulator, it would have to draw constant power at constant consumption. And this would tend to create a current function of the form: I(t)=P/(A*sin(2*Pi*f*t)) which would draw a large current at low voltage points to maintain constant power. Such a current function increases the effective current through the conductors and creates additional transmission losses.
The best point of consumption for the smallest current through the conductors is at the top of the sinusoidal function. And the best PFC corrector is an LC filter after the diode rectifier, which suppresses the high harmonics of impulse current disturbances, i.e. reduces the current peak and extends the duration.

PFC only makes sense on machines that have sinusoidal current consumption that is out of phase with the voltage. And these circuits are called reactive power compensators.

There is also no conclusion from the measurement that the installation of the PFC circuit increased the effective input current by more than 10%. Because of this, losses in electricity transmission increase by more than 20%.

candidates.reason: The comment directly discusses the topic of power factor correction (PFC) and its relevance to electricity measurement, mentioning specific examples like washing machines, pumps, and motors. This is a strong connection to the topic 'Conclusion' which summarizes PFC.
candidates.comment:
Interesting factoid about PFC: in the past, unscrupulous people used to tamper with their inductive loads, such as washing machines, pumps, and other motors and REMOVE the PFC capacitor in order to steal part of the electricity from the power company!
This is because power companies used to measure their customers' energy consumption using electromechanical meters, old devices containing a big spinning wheel that would complete a revolution after a known amount of energy was delivered to the customer, plus an odometer to count the wheel's revolutions.
One problem with those electromechanical meters (that has since been solved with digital energy meters) is that they would only measure the current delivered IN PHASE with the voltage. Large inductive loads, such as motors, were (and still are) required by law to be sold with a suitable capacitor as a passive PFC. But if one removed the capacitor, a good part of that load would become undetectable by the energy meter!
This is of course illegal and detrimental to the power grid, so nobody should attempt to do it, except in a laboratory condition.

The power factor initially was something like 0.95, then dropped to 0.87 or something like that once the tubes started conducting. I have seen DC chokes only on some tube radios (in some cases they use the output transformer as a choke), most devices do not have one and there was no problem with power factor until switching power supplies became prevalent.

candidates.comment:
From what I've read the real problem with uncorrected electronic power supplies is the amount of third harmonic current drawn, as in a three phase system the neutral current is supposed to cancel but the 3rd harmonics add.

One possible unfortunate unintended consequence is that with the power supply industry bragging about 0.98+ power factors in single phase equipment and crazy low harmonics it has caused a problem for the designers of multi-kilowatt systems.
It is easy to get a simple three phase rectifier to about 0.85, maybe 0.9 I can't remember the exact figure by just levelling the current drawn and sometimes an inductor is enough, but getting above that to the levels claimed for single phase designs is significantly more complicated. As a result installations that should be three-phase input end up using multiple single phase modules instead. Hopefully they are properly spread across phases.
